title: The conch from the sea
hookLine: Krishna wins back his teacher's drowned son and brings home a conch; why Hindus blow the shankha at worship
carry: the conch is breath offered as holy sound
tomorrow: the lamp blows out at dinner. what does Arjuna learn?
last: THE MOTHER COMES BACK, IN ANY FORM.

cards: When Krishna and his brother Balarama were boys, they went away to study with a teacher named Sandipani, in the city of Avanti. The story says they learned everything he had to teach in sixty-four days. Then came the fee.
A student traditionally gives the teacher a gift, guru dakshina, and Sandipani and his wife asked for the one thing no one could give: their son, who had drowned in the sea.

teach.h: PANCHAJANYA: THE CONCH FROM THE SEA.
teach.b: Krishna went to the shore. The ocean told him a demon named Panchajana, living in the shape of a conch shell, had taken the boy. Krishna went down and fought the demon, and found no boy inside.
So he took the demon's shell, went all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blew it. Yama came out, bowed, and gave the boy back.
That shell is Panchajanya, the conch Krishna blew at Kurukshetra, back on day seventy-six. This is from the Bhagavata Purana, and it sits under a sound you can still hear in Hindu homes and temples.
The shankha, the conch, is one of the four things Vishnu holds in his hands.

At the start of puja or aarti, someone blows a conch: breath turned into a sound that announces God is being welcomed, and, many say, clears the air. That's the teaching: even your breath can be an offering.
Krishna's reached the lord of death. Now a breath you can hear without a shell.
Ujjayi, usually translated as victorious, from ud, upward, and ji, to win. Teachers explain the name in different ways, and the texts don't settle it. Here's how it's done.
Open your mouth and breathe out as if fogging a mirror, haaa. Feel the slight catch in the throat? Close your mouth and keep that catch as you breathe out through the nose, then in.

teach.h: THE CONCH IS BREATH OFFERED AS HOLY SOUND.
teach.b: A soft ocean sound, only loud enough for you, the throat relaxed, never squeezed. Think of it as a quiet cousin of the conch.

how: Many Hindu homes and temples blow a conch (shankha) at the start of puja or aarti; the conch is one of the four emblems Vishnu holds. In yoga, ujjayi is breathing through the nose with a slight narrowing of the throat that makes a soft ocean sound, used in seated pranayama and posture practice.

games.q: at a temple, a kid asks why someone blows into a shell right before the aarti. what fits today's teaching?
o: it's the shankha, Vishnu's conch: breath turned into a holy sound to welcome God.
it's to wake up anyone dozing in the crowd.
it's a war signal, since conches were blown at Kurukshetra.
games.why: the conch is one of Vishnu's emblems, and its sound opens worship. Krishna's Panchajanya reached even the city of Yama.

practice: Open your mouth and breathe out as if fogging a mirror, haaa, then close your mouth and keep that soft catch in the throat as you breathe out and in through the nose.
Let it be slow, with the out-breath a little longer, and keep the sound only loud enough for you. Just listen to the waves.
